summary: The companion has a visible depth structure across the main reader-facing layers, and this audit records the evidence that should be checked before calling a page ready. The explicit source caveat is the one playlist item whose captions are not exposed by yt-dlp.

requirements.evidence: Standalone git repo at topology-geometry-course-concepts-research on main.

requirements.requirement: Recover all playlist links and source coverage
requirements.evidence: 35 playlist videos indexed; 34 caption files recovered; missing caption preserved for nx1XOlezuvk.

15 lecture explainers with full essay sections, lecture-deepening fields, slow walkthroughs, caption-nuance notes, problem, first principles, mathematical move, important detail, connection, transcript anchors, source-lens paragraphs, and examples.

Each lecture separates caption support from course-arc inference and caveat. That keeps a reader from mistaking a useful interpretation for a direct transcript claim, with 2462 words devoted to source-faithfulness checks.

15 lecture-source bridges explain how a concrete course demonstration connects to a wider source family without pretending the lecture cited that source word for word. The bridge layer has 5650 words across demonstration, mathematical bridge, source extension, overread warning, and reader-question fields.

Each lecture asks the reader to explain the object, check the allowed move, protect the conclusion, connect the lecture to outside use, and then compare against an answer guide. The 3416 reader-test words, 6390 lecture-application words, and 3817 answer-guide words turn lecture understanding into an auditable task.

15 reconstruction drills ask the reader to rebuild a lecture from example to object, legal move, surviving fact, later use, and source check. The 7380 reconstruction words test whether the lecture can be explained from its working parts rather than remembered as a title.

15 source-nuance repair notes name caption hazards, safe claims, repair moves, do-not-claim guards, evidence checks, and concept links. The 2775 repair words make source caution usable on actual lecture sentences.
15 lecture-spine entries name the object, plain question, legal move, surviving fact, and later use. The spine shows the course order as a chain of reasoning instead of a sequence of titles.

requirements.requirement: Hand-written concepts, themes, subthemes, and method families
requirements.evidence: 24 concepts, 6 themes, 10 subthemes, and 5 method families have essays plus first-principles fields. Concept pages tie ideas to anchor examples, outside-application checks, and self-checks; theme and subtheme pages now add 6250 application words; method-family pages add answer guides so the reader can use the idea, not only recognize its name. These cross-course answer guides add 10946 words, and concept applications add 10034 words.
Validation enforces minimum depth across all explanatory layers and blocks loose stock phrases; pages explain why ideas exist and what detail matters.

6 prose tests enforce the writing standard: object before term, legal move, protected fact, failure condition, course anchor, and everyday-language replacement. The rubric names what to repair when a paragraph sounds smooth but does not explain the mathematics.

The six quality tests are mapped across 6 layers: lectures, concepts, themes, subthemes, method families, and source/quality pages. That map tells where a failure belongs instead of letting a weak paragraph hide inside site-wide complexity.
45 lecture examples link forward to concepts; every concept links back to lecture appearances, with appearance counts from 2 to 20.
The Math Why page explains the course engine: allowed changes, preserved facts, designed counts, and whole-shape constraints.
The Math Playground page has four canvas widgets for Euler characteristic, signed cancellation, fixed points, and vector-field index.
The Course Synthesis page connects the lecture sequence, proof families, mathematical objects, operations, failure modes, and reader questions in one first-principles path.

8 dependency paths show why later theorems need earlier habits: legal motion, constructed spaces, orientation, protected counts, and state modeling. This prevents the course from reading as a flat list of topics.

6 application-spine rows explain why topology matters in outside fields by naming the plain problem, topological move, outside use, honest payoff, wrong reading, and reader test. The 1663 application words keep applications tied to first principles rather than loose comparisons.

8 transfer cases ask the reader to move the course habit into everyday situations by naming the object, allowed move, protected fact, wrong transfer, and reader task. The 2022 transfer words test whether the mathematics has become a usable way to think.

8 repair-clinic cases start with explanations that read smoothly but fail technically, then repair them by naming the missing object, move, protected evidence, or limit. The 1791 repair-clinic words make the no-filler standard concrete.

7 oral-exam prompts ask for explanations that can survive follow-up questions. The prompt, strong-answer, must-include, common-failure, and follow-up fields use 1551 words to test whether the reader can connect the course without hiding behind topic names.

10 change-ledger cases separate legal change from false motion. The 2081 words ask the reader to say what object changed, what fact survived, why the survival matters, and which tempting move would solve a different problem.

10 assumption-ledger cases expose the quiet conditions behind course claims. The 2012 words name the assumption, why it is needed, how to check it plainly, and where the argument breaks if the condition is missing.
10 counterexample cases show how a tempting sentence fails when a condition is missing. The 2012 words make failure scenes visible, then repair the claim so the reader sees the boundary of the idea.

10 weak course sentences are diagnosed and rewritten into first-principles versions. The 1934 repair words show the missing detail, where the stronger sentence belongs, and what must be checked before accepting it.

5 proof-move recipes turn repeated course habits into steps: set up the object, perform the legal move, protect the evidence, and state the limited conclusion. Each recipe includes why it works, how it fails, and a course example.

The Formula Reader turns seven central statements into plain readings: what object the formula speaks about, what operation produced the terms, why the quantity survives, what conclusion it can force, and what check prevents symbol-copying.

8 theorem-use contracts state when a theorem is allowed to speak. The 2679 words require the object, allowed move, protected evidence, conclusion, break condition, and everyday test before a theorem name can carry weight.

10 contrast pairs separate neighboring ideas that readers often blur. The 2269 words name the confusion, the left job, the right job, the bridge between them, and the failure test that catches a merged explanation.

requirements.requirement: Reader checks for common failure modes
requirements.evidence: The Reader Checks page gathers eleven course-wide mistakes and gives concrete replacement questions linked to lectures, concepts, method families, and the formula reader.

16 formal course words are translated into everyday sentences only after their job in an argument is named. The 3103 term-translation words include non-definition warnings, failure conditions, reader questions, and concept links so vocabulary does not replace understanding.

7 course, primary-paper, and standard-textbook sources are linked with lecture coverage, concept coverage, plain use notes, and source caveats. Lecture and concept pages carry their own source trails so references support claims without becoming unearned authority.

7 source-reader entries explain what problem each source helps with, what object to watch, how it bridges to the course, and what would overread it. The 2015 source-reader words keep paper reading tied to first-principles course questions.

7 paper-family contracts state the problem, object, allowed reading, protected idea, course bridge, overclaim boundary, and reader test for each source family. The 2014 words make the paper layer usable without letting it drown the course explanation.
